subject: mathematics
question_text: If A is the matrix with rows (i, 0) and (0, i), then find A².

recall_prompt: Say how you would find A squared here, and what the answer turns out to be.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Multiply A by A
steps.margin_note: First mark. A² means A × A. The matrix is diagonal, so each diagonal entry simply squares and the off-diagonal entries stay 0.
steps.memory_tip: A² means A × A. The matrix is diagonal, so each diagonal entry squares and the off-diagonals stay 0.

lines.text: A^2 = A \times A = \begin{bmatrix} i & 0 \\ 0 & i \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} i & 0 \\ 0 & i \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} i^2 & 0 \\ 0 & i^2 \end{bmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That A² is A multiplied by A, and that for this diagonal matrix the result has i² on the diagonal.
accept: A squared is A times A and since it is diagonal the entries become i squared
multiply the matrix by itself to get i squared on the diagonal
row into column multiplication gives i squared in both diagonal places
A into A cheste diagonal lo i square vasthundi
the off diagonal entries stay zero and the diagonal squares

steps.why: Even with complex entries, matrix multiplication is unchanged — row against column. Only the arithmetic inside the entries is new.
common_mistakes: Squaring the entries of a matrix that is not diagonal — entry-by-entry squaring works here only because the off-diagonal zeros make every cross term zero.
Assuming a diagonal matrix cannot be multiplied.

steps.label: Use i² = −1
steps.margin_note: Second mark, and the point of the question. i² = −1, so the matrix becomes −1 on the diagonal — which is exactly −I.
steps.memory_tip: i² = −1, so the diagonal becomes −1 — which is exactly −I.

recall.must_convey: That i² = −1, so A² becomes −1 on the diagonal, which is −I.
accept: i squared is minus one so the matrix is minus one on the diagonal which is minus I
using i squared equals minus one the answer is negative the identity matrix
A squared comes out as minus I
i square minus one kabatti A square equals minus I
the result is minus the identity matrix

steps.why: Writing the answer as −I rather than as a grid of −1s shows you recognised the identity matrix, which is what the question is really testing.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as a matrix of −1s without naming it −I.

insider_note: Both diagonal entries are i, so both square to −1 and A² = −I. The answer is the negative identity matrix, not the zero matrix.
